body: Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. Oil prices reversed their recent downtrend on Thursday, a day after Democrats swept control of both the House and Senate, creating a potential legislative check on U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration. Brent crude was up 4.0% to trade at $98.38 per barrel at 3:15 pm ET, while WTI gained 2.9% to $90.65, with prices rising for the first time in four sessions after plunging to a near two-month low on Wednesday. U.S. natural gas prices were flat at $2.95/MMBtu, while European gas prices rebounded 1.9% to €89.72/MWh. The U.S. stock market resumed its recent downtrend on Thursday, with the S&P 500 down more than 3% and the Nasdaq off about 5% in afternoon trading as a selloff in AI chip stocks deepened. AI stocks tied to Texas data centers were hit hard after Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated long-serving Texas governor Greg Abbott, with CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) falling 7% and Nebius Group (NASDAQ:NBIS) and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) each sliding 4% in overnight trading on Wednesday. Hinojosa has called for a pause on new data-center projects until protections for electricity supplies, water resources and local communities are in place, with investors fearing similar roadblocks could slow down the AI data center boom once Democratic governors take office in January 2027. The energy investment universe was a mixed bag, with the oil and gas benchmark, State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLE), falling 1.6% to $62.50 on Thursday, as energy stocks tracked the broader market lower despite the rebound in crude. Wednesday’s 8.7% plunge in Brent priced in bets that the election setback would force the Trump administration to pursue a peace deal with Iran and reopen Hormuz. Related: European Gas Prices Drop on Iran Deal Hopes after U.S. Midterms Those bets faded on Thursday , with Eurasia Group cutting its odds of a negotiated agreement to 10% from 20% and putting the likelihood of renewed U.S. strikes at 60%, while Iran’s navy reported that a tanker struck a mine east of the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire. President Trump acknowledged the war’s role in the Republican losses but said the conflict has been worth it. Additionally, Democratic committee chairs are set to deploy their new subpoena powers from January to investigate the administration’s energy dealings. Their targets include its Venezuelan oil concessions to North American Blue Energy Partners, critical mineral deals involving Cantor Fitzgerald, and the cancellation of nearly $8 billion in energy projects in states that voted for Kamala Harris. Separately, two of three Russian tankers carrying diesel to the U.S. under the Trump-Putin deal have abruptly changed course , one toward Brazil and the other into the Mediterranean. “It’s clear there’s hesitancy here in bringing these barrels onshore just because of the implications of doing so,” Kpler analyst Matt Smith said. The Middle East physical oil market has also flipped into a surplus for the first time since July, as crude exports from Arab Gulf producers surged. Combined shipments from Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq and Kuwait rose 10% to 15.53 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, nearing levels recorded at the start of the year. The numbers come from tanker-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg. Saudi Arabia raised exports 13% to 7 million bpd, with shipments from Yanbu on the Red Sea up 35% to 3.07 million bpd. Iraq shipped 3.35 million bpd, up 9.5%, and Kuwait increased exports by a third to 1.44 million bpd. Tanker-tracking data showed no Iranian crude exports for a second month under the U.S. naval blockade. Dubai crude for prompt delivery now trades below later-dated cargoes, a contango structure that means near-term supply exceeds demand. While signs have emerged that smaller independents have started to take advantage of the higher oil prices to increase drilling, the biggest shale producers are keeping their powder dry amid unprecedented uncertainty in global markets. One of the top shale producers and the biggest Permian-only focused driller, Diamondback Energy, signaled this week that it will not be splashing on materially increased drilling activity next year as uncertainty remains too high. So far this year, the WTI Crude price has averaged $86.72, more than $20 per barrel compared to the 2025 average of $64.94. The price spike alone is not a reason for loosening capital spending discipline, according to the biggest shale producers, including Diamondback. “I wouldn't say I'm unnecessarily cautious personally, but I think it's always good to prepare the company for a swing to the downside,” Diamondback’s chief executive Kaes Van't Hof told analysts on the Q3 earnings call earlier this week. Diamondback boosted third-quarter earnings, raised its 2026 dividend, and revised up slightly its production outlook for this year, as it generated $2.1 billion in free cash flow for Q3. “Base dividend growth remains a core tenet of the value proposition at Diamondback and our base dividend is now up over 9x since initiating at $0.50 per share in 2018,” Van't Hof wrote in the quarterly letter to shareholders. Diamondback has used excess cash to repurchase bonds and shares and reduce debt in recent months, while it remains cautious about splashing on boosting production. “The macro backdrop is almost exactly as we described last quarter: highly volatile and impossible to predict. The timing of the eventual global oil supply normalization is anyone’s guess, and we therefore expect the current volatility to continue,” Van't Hof told shareholders. “Through this volatility, our priorities remain unchanged: execute with the best capital efficiency in the industry and allocate Free Cash Flow appropriately to maximize long-term stockholder value.” At the earnings call, the executive said he was leaning into the ‘higher-for-longer’ camp of oil price expectations, “but we prepare the business to keep our cost structure low and execution in perfect shape because the inevitable can happen.” Van't Hof noted that “There's just still some uncertainty over the next couple months, and there's just not a need for us to put out a formal 2027 plan because we always end up doing that in February.” The macro picture is so muddied right now that not only Diamondback, but all other U.S. shale producers are unlikely to jump the gun on a significant drilling spree next year just because oil prices are high now. So far this year, U.S. oil production has increased slightly, but not at any scale to offset the massive disruption of supply from the Middle East. body: Asian countries that depend on oil and gas imports for their energy security are hoping that the results of the U.S. midterms will lead to an end to the war in the Middle East and, consequently, an end to the severe fuel crisis Asian countries are experiencing. The hopes may be premature, however. Trump is still president, and Democrats are no fans of Iran. Asia has been the hardest-hit by the fallout of the U.S. and Israel offensive against Iran that began on February 28. For geographical reasons, the Middle East is the top supplier of hydrocarbons to Asia. With that supplier largely gone for an extended period of time, Asian countries were scrambling to secure alternatives—at higher prices. This brought inflation and boosted government spending to try and shield the economy from the worst of the fallout. Last month, the World Bank warned that, essentially, Asia was running out of money because of the energy crisis. “Subsidies have been by far the most common policy response [to the crisis] among emerging and developing economies,” the World Bank said, adding that “Countries with substantial subsidies in place generally have had smaller increases in retail gasoline prices than non-subsidizers, but this relationship weakened considerably for headline inflation.” So, now that Democrats have won a majority in both the House and the Senate, there are hopes they would rein the U.S. president in, including on foreign policy. Reuters’s Clyde Russell wrote in a column this week that the way Democrats can interfere with Trump’s policies is to use congressional power to redirect, cut or boost government spending and to start investigations against Trump himself and close allies and family members. Whether that would be enough to bring down Asian diesel prices remains uncertain. What some observers expect the Democrats to do is ramp up financing for Ukraine at the expense of the Iran war, which will not really change anything with prices because it would simply mean more Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries while Iran remains unconvinced it could make a lasting peace with the United States. Related: European Gas Prices Drop on Iran Deal Hopes after U.S. Midterms This suggests Asian economies are not about to get any fast relief on fuels and other petroleum derivatives, just because the Democrats won 240 seats in the House, versus 147 for the Republicans, and 54 seats in the Senate, versus 44 for the Republicans. In fact, chances are nothing will change much, not fast, anyway. And this means pain at the pump—and everywhere else—will continue. For now, hopes seem to be running high that Democrats will somehow manage to push Trump to make peace with Iran. The details on how exactly remain unclear, but oil prices crashed below $100 on Wednesday following the results of the midterms. This suggests traders are now anticipating an end to the hostilities somehow orchestrated by the Democrat-dominated two houses of parliament. However, some geopolitical analysts have warned that Trump may try to compensate for the election loss at home with an escalation against Iran. Indeed, several analysts from the Middle East have, as cited by Reuters, suggested that an escalation could be Trump’s only option to save face. This does not bode well for Asian economies and, by extension, the rest of the world. Asia was considered the powerhouse of the developing world, the continent where much of the world’s economic growth was taking place and would continue to take place in the coming years. The war has prompted revisions to these forecasts, with fears of recession running high despite delicate phrasing by forecasters. Hopes for a shift in U.S. policies are therefore quite understandable—if possibly misplaced. title: New gold discovery boosts Perpetua’s Stibnite project
summary: Fiddle’s discovery hole returned 109.7 meters grading 3.2 g/t gold and 1.1% antimony, among the most significant mineralized intercepts encountered at the project, the company said.
body: Perpetua Resources (Nasdaq: PPTA) (TSX: PPTA) said it has made a new gold discovery during its 2026 exploration drilling program at its Stibnite Gold project in central Idaho, with over 16,000 meters of core drilling across the project now completed. Perpetua Resources is advancing construction on the $1.3 billion Stibnite Gold project in central Idaho, which was fast-tracked by the Trump administration as part of efforts to strengthen the US critical minerals supply chain. The Stibnite project is set to produce roughly 450,000 ounces of gold annually, supported by proven and probable reserves of 148 million pounds of antimony and more than six million ounces of gold. It is one of the few known US sources of antimony, a mineral essential to defence systems, energy storage, and semiconductors, and one of the largest deposits outside China’s control. Fiddle’s discovery hole, SB633, returned 109.7 meters grading 3.2 g/t gold and 1.1% antimony, among the most significant mineralized intercepts encountered at the project to date, the company said. Located approximately 750 meters south of the permitted Yellow Pine pit along the Meadow Creek Fault Zone, Fiddle adds a new target area to the project’s growing in-pit and near-pit resource base. The north-trending MCFZ is the district’s main ore-controlling structure, which runs through both the Yellow Pine and Hangar Flats deposits and hosts intrusive-hosted mineralization along its flanks. To test the structural controls of the MCFZ, three holes were subsequently drilled, Perpetua said. This included SB637, which extended mineralization to the north and returned 37.4 meters grading 0.7 g/t gold, 0.1% antimony from 93.8 meters downhole. Initial assays from the Fiddle target returned 109.7 meters grading 3.2 g/t gold, 1.1% antimony in hole SB633, beginning at 189 meters downhole. SB633 represents one of the broadest continuous intervals of gold and antimony mineralization returned to date from Stibnite while also exhibiting grades more than double the project’s life-of-mine average. An additional 21 holes were drilled along strike of SB633. Core logging identified both holes as having similar style mineralization to hole SB633, including abundant stibnite and sulfides within the mineralized zones. Follow-up drilling from the Clark Tunnel Fault Zone continued to demonstrate near-surface, high grades including 25.4 meters of 4.5 g/t gold from 13 meters downhole (SB606) and 25.0 meters of 2.3 g/t gold from 18 meters downhole (SB605), the company said. “Given their close proximity to the permitted Yellow Pine pit, Fiddle and the CTFZ were prioritized as key targets for the 2026 exploration program,” Perpetua CEO Jon Cherry said in a news release . “At Fiddle, our initial hole returned broad, continuous mineralization at significant gold and antimony grades which confirm it as an important new discovery. Meanwhile, drilling continues to reinforce the CTFZ as a near-surface, high-grade target on the eastern extent of the Yellow Pine pit,” Cherry said. body: The country’s economic outlook makes for grim reading – with two major exceptions F inancial markets and economists were of one mind that the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) would this week announce yet another rate hike, its fifth in this cycle, and they did. But it’s probably worth focusing on the fact that three of the nine monetary board members voted to keep rates on hold. To be clear, it’s likely the dissenters agreed that inflation remains too high at present: it clearly is. Underlying inflation, the best indicator of price pressures, has been outside the RBA’s target band (of 2% to 3%) for almost all of the past four years . The dissenters may well have been equally uncomfortable with the increase in inflationary expectations, which jumped up to 5.3% in October. When people expect inflation to be higher, it can allow businesses to more easily pass on price increases – a vicious cycle. Rather, as the governor made clear in her press conference after the decision was announced, the three mavericks felt that the downside risks to the economy from previous rate rises (and likely many other factors) were already large and that yet another increase would risk leaving the Australian economy too weak. The RBA disagrees and thinks the upside risks to inflation are the main game. The press conference showed little nuance, or even respect, for those downside risks. Economics is always about tradeoffs. Since the pandemic, the RBA has tried to stay on its “narrow path”, balancing growth (and employment) goals against inflation targets. With both inflation and unemployment rising, it’s hard to say they are achieving either goal – but hindsight is a wonderful thing. So now our central bankers are telling us there’s to be no more mollycoddling: we will take our medicine until we recover, and it’s bitter medicine indeed. The RBA’s latest forecasts in the accompanying November statement on monetary policy make for some grim reading. Overall economic growth is now expected to slow from 1.6% this financial year to just 1.3% over 2027-28. That implies that growth in per capita GDP (our individual slice of the collective economic pie) will, at best, be flat. Meanwhile, the overall pie only increases as a result of population growth. Along with the slower growth outlook comes higher unemployment, which is expected to hit 5.1% by 2028. This seems to be a rather rosy outlook in my view. Real wages will fall further than previously forecast, as will productivity. Across the economy, the numbers look a lot weaker, with two notable exceptions. The first is, not unexpectedly, public sector demand, which has been left broadly unchanged. No doubt the federal treasurer will continue to face calls to find ways to cut spending (the states are conveniently being overlooked). As an aside, notice it’s automatically assumed that if it’s public sector, it must be “bad” spending, but if it’s private sector, it must be “good”. All that wasteful spending on education, health, our older and less able citizens, not to mention transport. Business investment, on the other hand, gets a free pass, totally unexamined. Business investment is the second area of the forecasts that has been, quite strongly, upgraded – largely the result of datacentre builds. In terms of the economy (as measured by GDP), the datacentres don’t make much of a difference – the imports required to build them count as a negative in our economic accounting system. But datacentres do matter for inflation; the RBA governor even flagged this in her post-meeting conference. The current mantra of proceed at speed on datacentre rollouts comes at a huge cost. Just as the mining boom in the 2000s saw kids ditching education for large wages in the resources sector, this decade our construction workers and tradies – even apprentices – are being enticed to work on datacentres at salaries of multiple what they would get in the residential sector. title: SanDisk Plunges 22% in a Single Day as AI Data Center Regulatory Risk Swallows Up '378% Revenue Surge' - BigGo Finance
body: SanDisk (SNDK), whose earnings have surged on demand for AI data center storage, was tripped up by a political variable: the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections. On the Nasdaq on Nov. 5 (local time), SanDisk shares closed at $806.43, down 22.26% from the prior session. That decline stands out against Micron's 17.16% drop and Western Digital's 17.39% slide the same day. With the Nasdaq Composite down about 5.5%, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) fell more than 11%, its worst day since March 2020. The trigger for the selloff was politics, not earnings. With Democrats winning both the Senate and the House and also prevailing in key gubernatorial races, fears have grown over tighter regulation of AI data center construction. The calculation that expansion schedules could be delayed by power and water procurement and permitting issues—pushing back orders for NAND Flash and SSDs—stripped buying interest from the sector broadly. The earnings themselves beat market expectations. SanDisk's fiscal 2027 first-quarter revenue, disclosed on Oct. 29, came in at $11.031 billion, up 378% year over year and 23% quarter over quarter. Data center revenue was $4.802 billion, up 61% from the prior quarter and accounting for about 44% of total revenue. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) improved to $49.51 from $39.25 in the prior quarter. According to the company, about 60% of the quarter-over-quarter revenue increase came from higher volume and 40% from higher prices. Guidance for the next quarter also assumes continued growth. The company projected revenue of $12.2 billion to $12.6 billion and adjusted EPS of $55 to $57. Consumer business revenue, however, fell 29% quarter over quarter to $397 million, revealing a phase in which the market is adjusting to higher prices. CEO David Goeckeler said at the time of the earnings release, "We started fiscal 2027 with another strong quarter, and as product demand grew solidly, our data center business drove faster growth." The problem is valuation. SanDisk shares had climbed more than 450% year to date through Oct. 29, and the recent plunge has pulled them about 65% off their peak of $2,354. Even so, the year-to-date gain still exceeds 250%. After such a run-up, the stock is structurally vulnerable to any single signal of slowing AI investment or a peak in memory prices. RBC Capital cut its price target to $1,400 from $1,600 the day after the earnings release and maintained its "Sector Perform" rating. The revision reflected a decline in valuation multiples across the memory sector, even though results and guidance exceeded expectations. The episode illustrates the volatility of the entire AI infrastructure investment cycle rather than a problem specific to SanDisk. Given that earnings surged on the combination of strong NAND prices and data center expansion, the key variable for the stock's direction going forward is whether customer orders and long-term supply contracts are carried out as scheduled even if the policy environment changes. The fact that the semiconductor sector broadly saw a double-digit correction in a single day also suggests that regulatory risk is not confined to any one stock.

The two developments tell different stories. One is about where Vertiv wants to be in five years. The other is about what the market is willing to pay for that ambition today. Their economic weight will determine whether the expansion genuinely broadens the company or merely decorates the pitch. Hassett, on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," acknowledged the dozens of measures on states' midterm ballots seeking to constrain data centers, a crucial part of President Donald Trump 's push to win the global artificial intelligence race. In at least 46 of the at least 50 such initiatives on ballots in 2026, majorities voted to restrict development of the facilities, according to Ballotpedia's tally. "We respect the localities that decide that's what they want to do," Hassett said. "But America is a big place, and right now, the data centers scheduled over the next couple of years aren't affected by these ballot initiatives." "And the stuff after that, you know, there's plenty of room in the U.S. for data center growth to continue, as it was projected ahead of the election," he said. Hassett said he expects data centers will continue to expand in states with more welcoming governors, and he suggested that even hostile states will eventually come around. "That's exactly what's going to happen," he said. "That, or what'll happen will be that the benefits of the data centers will be so obvious that people decide to change their minds about the way they regulate them." Hassett also blamed Thursday's tech-driven market plunge on "uncertainty about what the political change is going to mean for data centers going forward." "But I think that the economic strength that we see everywhere else is so strong, and of course, in the end, you could take something that's growing as fast as the data centers and make it grow a little bit slower, and you still have a blockbuster economy." "And so, I think we're still very, very optimistic about what's going to happen going forward," he said. title: Family offices boost startup investments in October, backing women's health and caregivers
summary: Laurene Powell Jobs' Emerson Collective was the most active family-office investor with three startup bets.
body: After a slow September, investment firms of ultra-wealthy families stepped up their deal-making last month. In October, family offices made 56 direct investments in companies, up about 30% from the month prior, according to data provided exclusively to CNBC by Fintrx, a private wealth intelligence platform. Laurene Powell Jobs' Emerson Collective was the most prolific investor of the month, backing three healthcare startups according to Fintrx data. Her investment and philanthropy firm seeks to address health equity and other complex challenges like the energy transition. Last month, Emerson Collective joined a $555 million Series G for Devoted Health, a healthcare provider and insurer of Medicare Advantage plans, alongside information technology billionaire Azim Premji's namesake family office. Devoted Health, which has counted Emerson Collective as an investor since 2021, announced that it will use the fundraise to expand to five additional states for a total of 34. Powell Jobs' firm also participated in two fundraises for healthcare data startups BioStack and Collective X Health. BioStack, which raised $9.5 million in seed funding, analyzes patient records across different institutions to create training datasets for artificial intelligence healthcare models. Collective X Health, fresh off a $3.2 million pre-seed round, seeks to close the gender data gap by compiling and licensing peer-reviewed, female-specific data and research. Emerson Collective is in good company as family offices continue to invest in healthcare innovations from telehealth to drug discovery. In a family office survey released by Citi Wealth in September, healthcare ranked as the second-most-popular sector for direct investing at 32%, only behind AI at 51%. Melinda French Gates' Pivotal Ventures joined an $82 million Series C for Abby Care, an AI-enabled startup that trains and certifies family members as paid caregivers under Medicaid and Medicare programs. Erin Harkless Moore, who manages investments at Pivotal Ventures, told CNBC that the firm looks for founders who have first-hand experience with the complexities of healthcare. Abby Care CEO and founder Havi Nguyen started navigating the Medicaid system at age 9 as a caregiver for her sisters and eventually her grandparents. "We look for teams that understand the problem deeply and have a model built for the realities of the healthcare system as it currently exists. Abby Care is a great example," Moore said. "Their deep understanding of the market allowed them to both spot an unsolved problem and understand how to navigate the regulatory challenges in this space." For family offices looking to invest in healthcare, Moore said overlooked markets offer a chance to back companies addressing needs that have long gone unmet. "Women's health is a space that has been historically underfunded and under-researched. We have less data, less funding, and huge gaps to fill," she said. "That can make investing more challenging, but it can also point to where there's real opportunity."

body: The University of Michigan’s Surveys of Consumers is one of the oldest measures of US household sentiment but it's lost its lustre in financial markets due to readings that don't correspond with spending. The preliminary reading is released at 10 am ET in the first half of each month, based on interviews conducted over the preceding weeks. A final reading incorporating the full sample follows near the end of the month. The preliminary figure sometimes draws a market reaction because it’s the first look at the month. The headline Index of Consumer Sentiment is built from questions about personal finances, business conditions and whether it’s a good time to buy big-ticket items. It’s indexed to 100 in early 1966. The survey splits into two sub-indexes, current economic conditions and consumer expectations. The expectations measure is a component of the Conference Board’s Leading Economic Index. Inflation expectations are lately the most market-sensitive part of the release and the Fed will be pleased with the dip in today's report. Respondents estimate price changes over the next year and over the next five to 10 years. The Federal Reserve watches the longer-run measure as a signal of whether inflation expectations remain anchored, and sharp moves can shift Treasury yields and rate pricing. Because the preliminary sample is smaller, these figures can be revised meaningfully in the final release. The survey moved from telephone to online interviews in 2024, complicating comparisons with its long history. Responses have also become increasingly partisan, with sentiment swinging sharply depending on which party controls the White House. Sentiment readings don’t always match spending, and households often keep buying even when they say they’re pessimistic. Still, the survey provides a timely read on how consumers are reacting to inflation, tariffs, gasoline prices, the job market and stock prices. Despite the recovery of crude oil flows from the Gulf via Hormuz to nearly pre-war levels, buyers continue to struggle with scarce vessel availability and last-minute decisions by shipowners not to brave the Strait to load crude oil from inside the Persian Gulf. “The main challenge has been hiring of ships. The increased flows of oil from the Strait of Hormuz, mostly thanks to ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman, are tying up supertankers for weeks waiting for the transfers outside the Strait, limiting the availability of very large crude carriers (VLCCs) for the other global key oil trade routes. The inefficient oil loadings in the Middle East and the very tight supertanker market resulting from these have created a ripple effect extending to the market of smaller vessels, Aframax and Suezmax, whose demand and daily rates have also surged amid a shortage of supertankers. Sky-high rates add millions of U.S. dollars to the cost of a single crude oil cargo, further fueling oil and fuel prices. title: World embraces gold while US resists shift, advisor says
summary: In uncertain times, governments outside of the G7 are increasingly turning to gold as a safeguard against future financial crises.
body: Central banks outside the G7 are increasingly turning to gold to protect their economies from mounting debt and geopolitical uncertainty, while Western governments remain reluctant to challenge the US dollar’s dominance, according to Canaccord Genuity Wealth Management senior investment advisor Cam Currie. Currie, who also leads the Currie Metals & Mining Group, said countries are accumulating bullion as concerns grow over the management of Western economies which seem to refuse to accept a gold standard. “What we’re seeing here is the rest of the world is going to a gold standard,” Currie told host Adrian Pocobelli on The Northern Miner Podcas t. “So, they’re going back to a gold standard because they’re looking at the stewardship of the G7 countries and how mismanaged it is.” For Currie, countries outside of the G7 are looking to gold as a way to have some security. The non-yielding metal has become a reserve currency for these countries and is being used as leverage, he said. “The western world has not really embraced it because of course embracing it is suggesting there’s something wrong with the US dollar and that’s just not going to happen in our world given what’s going on right now,” Currie added. “But that’s what’s happening.” He suggested central banks have little incentive to publicly endorse a return to the gold standard while they continue building their holdings. “If you’re still buying it, which these central banks are, why would you want to announce you’re going to a gold standard, right? You’re still in the accumulation stage,” he said. Currie believes that rising debt levels and higher interest rates are making gold increasingly attractive as a safe-haven asset, making the metals gain a new place in the discussion. “That’s why gold has to be part of your asset class because there is a risk building in the debt markets,” he added. Despite the longer-term case for bullion, Currie believes it all comes down to how the story is being told and what is happening. He noted that when a narrative disappears, money also tends to go elsewhere. “The narrative right now is playing against us and that’s the opportunity. Price action creates narrative and narrative creates ETF flows,” he said. “The price action is negative, the narrative is negative, therefore, the ETF flows are negative.” Currie argued that investors should be making moves. They risk missing an eventual shift toward gold if they wait for concerns about government debt to become more widespread. For him the downside is not making a move now while everything is ‘on sale.’ “The question I have is when are people going to get really concerned about the debt problems and when that happens that’s when the real movement into gold in the western world will really escalate,” Currie said. “And like I said it’s two months from now, two years from now you don’t want to be sitting here looking ‘oh I knew it was going to happen but I never did anything about it.’” The eligible miners are still required to keep at least 30% of the proceeds in the onshore financial system for at least three months.

body: Oil Traders Want U.S. to Release Sanctioned Tankers as Freight Costs Soar Rystad Energy is an independent energy consulting services and business intelligence provider offering global databases, strategic advisory and research products for energy companies and suppliers,… For more than half a century, Norway’s oil and gas production has been underpinned by a handful of very large discoveries, the last of which, Wisting in the Barents Sea, was made more than a decade ago. Since then, exploration on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS) has increasingly focused on smaller finds close to existing infrastructure, allowing operators to bring new volumes online faster and at lower cost. While this approach has helped sustain production in the near term, it will not be enough to arrest the NCS’s projected decline through to 2040. Rystad Energy's base-case outlook indicates that production will fall short by 1.9 million barrels of oil equivalent per day (boepd) by 2040, highlighting the scale of the challenge facing the country's upstream sector. The outlook could deteriorate further if exploration activity does not increase. If exploration volumes over the next decade remain at the same level as the previous ten years, the production gap in 2040 would reach 2.2 million boepd. Halving the time taken to bring discoveries into production under the same exploration assumptions would reduce this to 2.1 million boepd, demonstrating that faster development alone will have a limited impact on the long-term outlook. Even doubling exploration volumes from the previous decade's level, while halving development timelines, would leave a shortfall of 1.4 million boepd. By comparison, Rystad Energy's base-case outlook, incorporating its own exploration assumptions, projects a production gap of 1.9 million boepd in 2040. These scenarios highlight the importance of increasing exploration activity, particularly through wildcat drilling targeting larger, higher-risk prospects away from existing infrastructure. While infrastructure-led exploration (ILX) will remain important for sustaining near-term production, it is unlikely to deliver the volumes needed to reverse the longer-term decline. The danger for Norway is that it becomes increasingly efficient at finding smaller volumes while losing the ability to replace the large fields that underpin its production base. If this continues, the country faces not only a steep decline in oil and gas output, but also a shrinking pipeline of major projects needed to sustain activity across the NCS. Reversing that trajectory requires operators to take on greater exploration risk and pursue more high-impact prospects capable of supporting standalone developments, rather than focusing predominantly on smaller tiebacks. The government must support this shift by ensuring access to fresh acreage and providing the conditions needed to encourage investment in higher-risk exploration, Tore Gulbrandsoy, Partner & Head of Stavanger, Rystad Energy. Norway’s challenge is not a lack of resources or the economics of exploration, but its declining ability to make large discoveries capable of sustaining production over the long term. Every offshore discovery exceeding 1 billion barrels of oil equivalent (boe) was made between 1969 and 2010. Since 2016, exploration has yielded around 3.2 billion boe, averaging just 320 million boe annually. At this rate, it would take more than 30 years to discover the estimated 11 billion boe still waiting to be found. This is despite Norway holding 31.7 billion boe in remaining offshore resources and achieving a 60% exploration success rate, above the global average of 55.5%. The problem is the size of discoveries: each successful wellbore adds around 7 million boe, compared with 18.4 million boe globally. JP Morgan sees global oil surplus at 1.4mn bpd in October; global oil stocks did not fall in September-October, Goldman says; Brent swaps curve changes structure to suggest ample supply; Brent futures curve still suggests tight prompt market The global oil market is showing signs of a return to excess supply as demand drops due to high prices, analysts and traders said, despite the lack of a resolution to the Iran war, which has disrupted exports from the Middle East since March. The market was widely expected at the start of 2026 to be in a surplus, but the outbreak of the Iran war in late February led to what the International Energy Agency called the world's biggest ever supply disruption and cut Middle East exports, overturning the surplus projections. Banks and government forecasters have cut global oil demand forecasts in 2026 in part due to high prices. As supplies recover, weak demand is helping the market to balance. Recovering Middle Eastern oil flows, rising production from other countries and weak demand have pushed global supply above consumption once again, JP Morgan said in a report. "We estimate the global oil market returned to a surplus of 1.1mn barrels per day in September, widening to 1.4mn bpd in October, nearly matching last year’s average of 1.3mn bpd," the bank said. Global crude oil imports in October rose above average 2025 levels, the bank said, while demand lags. The Iran war prompted the IEA to arrange a record release of oil from industrialised nations' strategic reserves, and has drawn down commercial inventories. However, Goldman Sachs estimates that global stocks did not decline in September to October after falling sizeably in the months following the start of the Iran war. Goldman sees the market as broadly balanced in the September-October period, compared to a deficit in March this year. A marginal surplus from last year, an uptick in production outside the Gulf, along with a decline in demand helped balance the market, the bank said. Both banks also pointed to an uptick of oil flows from the Middle East since the early months of the war. Oil shipments from the region edged lower in October from September's levels, which were the highest since the Iran war started. Two ship-tracking firms said the October figures could be revised upwards as more details on shipments emerge. Crude and condensate exports from the Gulf averaged 14mn bpd in October, or about 86% of pre-war levels, while refined product exports averaged 3.1mn bpd, or just over half of normal volumes, ship-tracking firm Vortexa said. In a sign of a short-term surplus of supply in the physical market, the price curve of Brent swaps, called contracts for differences, has moved. The contract for delivery this week is trading below that for the following week and at the steepest discount since July, according to LSEG data. The prices of the second- and third-week contracts are also trading at a discount to the next week. This market structure is called contango and generally reflects a perception that supply for immediate delivery is ample. By contrast, Brent crude futures starting from January 2027 delivery remain in the opposite structure to contango, known as backwardation, where prompt prices are higher than later contracts. This indicates that supply remains tight in the near term.
